newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Strong imports to widen UK Sept trade gap.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Strong imports to widen UK Sept trade gap.

text.p: Britain's trade gap with the rest of the world is expected to have widened sharply in September because strong domestic demand boosted imports, analysts said.

Figures for worldwide trade in September and non-EU trade in October are both due at 0930 GMT on Wednesday. A Reuter consensus of economists forecasts the worldwide trade deficit will stretch to 1.0 billion stg from 584 million in August.
The non-European Union trade deficit is forecast to shrink to 800 million stg in October from 851 million in September.
Economists are divided over whether non-EU trade will grow or shrink, but agree the movement is likely to be small.

"Notwithstanding any unexpected movement in the erratics (ships, aircraft and precious stones) balance, the non-EU trade deficit is likely to remain little changed in October, in line with the underlying trend," said Schroders' UK economist David Philpotts.
As for the global trade figure, September non-EU figures released last month give plenty of clues.
"Figures have already been released showing a slight rise in the UK's trade gap with non-EU countries in September," said Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers.
"We expect this swing to be supplemented by a slight deterioration in the UK's trade balance with other EU countries from the unusual 15 million sterling surplus recorded in August," he added.
Large growth in the September deficit would be due partly to a surprisingly small deficit in August when import volumes fell 2.1 percent, analysts said.

"August's deficit benefited from a surprise surplus with the EU, partly due to a higher erratics surplus, but also due to a fall in imports, unlikely to be sustained given strong domestic demand," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Retail sales data released last week showed a month-on-month rise of 0.4 percent, in line with expectations, suggesting confidence among British consumers continues to grow.
Barr forecast a 1.1 billion trade deficit in September, as did Philpotts.
"We expect to see import growth resume in September, as already suggested by the more timely non-EU data, taking the total deficit back out to 1.1 billion," said Philpotts.
Economists also said sterling's recent appreciation would push up British export prices and damage the attractiveness of British goods abroad in the near term.
"Although export growth is also relatively strong, this is at risk in coming months from the feedthrough of sterling strength," Barr said.
